coverage.headline: Top Noteworthy Copyright Stories from July 2026 — Hachette v. Google
coverage.summary: The Copyright Alliance's monthly roundup highlighted the July 10 Hachette v. Google filing as a key development, noting the complaint covers both direct copyright infringement and removal/alteration of Copyright Management Information (CMI) claims. The piece also flagged that the proposed class covers works sourced for limited purposes through Google Play Books and other Google services, as well as works scraped from pirate sources and paywalled websites.

coverage.headline: Publishers Sue Google Over Gemini Training on Copyrighted Books
coverage.summary: This piece emphasized the suit's allegation that an internal Google document warned the company that using copyrighted books for AI training could expose it to potential fines estimated in the tens to hundreds of billions of dollars. It also noted that two earlier California court decisions in the Anthropic and Meta cases found training on copyrighted books was likely fair use, setting up a critical circuit-level tension.

coverage.headline: The Copyright Info Google Allegedly Erased to Hide Gemini's Training
coverage.summary: Analysis of the publishers' July 10 complaint focuses on the DMCA copyright-management-information removal claim — that Google stripped authorship and ownership data from ingested books to conceal training sources — and contextualizes it against the 2025 Kadrey v. Meta ruling dismissing a similar claim.

coverage.headline: Book Writers Sue Google Over Alleged Use of Copyrighted Books to Train Gemini
coverage.summary: The complaint alleges four legal claims — direct copyright infringement, contributory copyright infringement, removal or alteration of copyright-management information, and DMCA violations — and cites an internal Google employee warning estimating potential fines of $10 billion to $100 billion.

coverage.headline: Publishers Sue Google Over Copyrighted Books Allegedly Used to Train Gemini
coverage.summary: BetaNews detailed the proposed class structure, noting it would cover owners of registered copyrights in books identified by ISBNs and journal articles identified by DOIs or ISSNs, provided Google copied those works from one of its services or used them for Gemini training. Plaintiffs seek statutory damages, destruction of infringing datasets, and an accounting of all works and methods used in Gemini's development.

coverage.headline: Book Publishers Sue Google For Copyright Infringement Over Gemini AI Training
coverage.summary: Slashdot aggregated Guardian reporting that publishers argue Google repurposed books supplied for limited services—such as displaying searchable snippets or selling ebooks via Google Play—not for copying into commercial AI training. The complaint illustrates market-harm claims by noting Gemini can generate a 100-page novel in 20 minutes for 39 cents, directly substituting for original works.

coverage.headline: Publishers sue Google over alleged use of books to train AI models
coverage.summary: Multiple book publishers sued Google in U.S. federal court in New York for allegedly copying copyrighted works to train Gemini and then generating content that directly competes with human authors. The plaintiffs requested an injunction and unspecified damages, with the complaint arguing Gemini can produce a 100-page book in 20 minutes for $0.39, a scale no publisher or author can match.

coverage.headline: Authors, publishers sue Google over alleged AI copyright infringement
coverage.summary: Hachette Book Group, Cengage Learning, Elsevier, and Scott Turow filed suit in a New York federal court alleging Google copied their works without disclosure to train Gemini. A technology IP attorney noted the suit's theory that any fair-use defense could be undermined by Google's alleged unlawful acquisition of the books.

coverage.headline: Hachette and Elsevier Sue Google for Using Their Work to Train AI
coverage.summary: Gizmodo reports that the publishers allege Gemini can generate content — including full-length novels and textbook-style explainers — that directly competes with original works, and that the same plaintiff group had already sued Meta over its Llama models earlier in 2026.

coverage.headline: Google Faces Another AI Training Lawsuit From Major Publishers
coverage.summary: TechCrunch reported that Hachette, Cengage, Elsevier, Scott Turow, and S.C.R.I.B.E. sued Google for using copyrighted works to train Gemini, with the complaint also alleging Google intentionally removed or altered copyright management information to conceal that its models were trained on the disputed materials. The suit follows a failed attempt by Hachette and Cengage to intervene in a separate California class action against Google.

coverage.headline: Google Faces Another AI Copyright Suit By Publishers
coverage.summary: Book publishers including Hachette, Cengage, and Elsevier, along with author Scott Turow, filed a copyright infringement suit alleging Google used their works to train its Gemini AI model. The suit follows an earlier action the same plaintiffs launched against Meta.

coverage.headline: Google Faces Fresh Copyright Lawsuit Over Gemini AI Training
coverage.summary: The complaint alleges Google stripped or altered copyright management information to conceal that Gemini was trained on unauthorized material sourced from Google Books, pirate websites, and paywalled platforms. Because the case is in New York rather than Northern California, a different court will rule on fair-use questions than the one handling the consolidated In re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation.

coverage.headline: U.S. Publishers Sue Google, Alleging Massive Copyright Infringement Behind Its Gemini AI Service
coverage.summary: The lawsuit accuses Google of illegally copying millions of works to train Gemini, which publishers argue is already flooding the marketplace with "AI-generated substitutes" that directly compete with human-authored books.

coverage.headline: Book Publishers Sue Google Over AI Training
coverage.summary: The suit, first reported by Publishers Weekly, seeks an injunction and statutory damages on behalf of a proposed class of authors and publishers, adding legal pressure to a broader publisher revolt against AI companies' use of copyrighted content.

coverage.headline: Publishers and Authors File Class Action Lawsuit Against Google for Willful Copyright Infringement to Develop Gemini AI Models
coverage.summary: Hachette Book Group, Cengage Learning, Elsevier, and author Scott Turow filed a putative class action in the S.D.N.Y. (1:26-cv-05870) alleging Google willfully infringed millions of textual works to develop its Gemini large language models. Plaintiffs bring claims on behalf of a proposed class of authors and publishers whose works were allegedly repurposed without authorization.

coverage.headline: Publishers, Authors File Class Action Lawsuit Against Google
coverage.summary: Hachette Book Group, Cengage Learning, Elsevier, and Scott Turow filed suit against Google seeking to block ongoing copyright infringement in the development of Gemini AI models, alleging it displaces legitimate book sales and threatens the growing content-licensing market. The plaintiffs withdrew their earlier motion to intervene in the 2023 California case to preserve broader claims and avoid statute-of-limitations issues.

coverage.headline: Publishers and Authors File Class Action Lawsuit Against Google for Willful Copyright Infringement to Develop Gemini AI Models
coverage.summary: The AAP announced that Hachette, Cengage, Elsevier, and Scott Turow filed a putative class action against Google for willful infringement of millions of textual works used to develop Gemini, after the publishers' earlier effort to intervene in the existing N.D. California class action did not proceed.

coverage.headline: Hachette Book Group Inc. et al v. Google LLC (case docket)
coverage.summary: Law360 tracks the newly filed copyright infringement suit by book publishers and novelist Scott Turow alleging Google used their works to train its Gemini AI model, following an earlier suit the same plaintiffs launched against Meta.
